lessons.title: Probability Foundations
lessons.concept: Probability measures how likely an event is. In equally likely outcomes, probability of event E is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the total number of possible outcomes in the sample space.
lessons.worked_example: A fair die is rolled. Sample space S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, so n(S)=6. Event E = getting an even number = {2,4,6}, n(E)=3. Therefore P(E)=3/6=1/2.
mistakes: Using outcomes that are not equally likely without adjusting the model
Counting favorable or total outcomes incorrectly
Reporting probability greater than 1 or less than 0

lessons.title: Complementary and Union Events
lessons.concept: The complement of event E (E') means E does not occur. For mutually exclusive events (cannot happen together), probabilities add. For events that can overlap, subtract the intersection once to avoid double counting.
lessons.formula: P(E') = 1 - P(E); mutually exclusive: P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B); general: P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A and B)
lessons.worked_example: From numbers 1-10, probability of a multiple of 2 is 5/10 and of a multiple of 5 is 2/10; overlap {10} is 1/10. So P(multiple of 2 or 5)=5/10+2/10-1/10=6/10=3/5.
mistakes: Adding probabilities of overlapping events without subtracting intersection
Forgetting complement is often easier when asked for 'at least one' in simple cases

lessons.title: Independent and Dependent Events
lessons.concept: Events are independent if one does not affect the probability of the other. For independent events, multiply probabilities for 'and'. When outcomes affect future probabilities (without replacement), events are dependent and conditional probabilities must be used.
lessons.formula: Independent: P(A and B)=P(A)*P(B). Dependent: P(A and B)=P(A)*P(B|A)
lessons.worked_example: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. With replacement, P(red then blue)= (3/5)*(2/5)=6/25. Without replacement, P(red then blue)= (3/5)*(2/4)=6/20=3/10.
mistakes: Not updating total/favorable counts after a dependent draw
Multiplying when events are mutually exclusive alternatives in a single trial

practice.explanation: Sample space = {Head, Tail}, total outcomes = 2, favorable = 1. Probability = 1/2.

practice.question: A card is drawn at random from a standard deck of 52 cards. What is the probability of drawing a king?
practice.explanation: There are 4 kings in 52 cards. Probability = 4/52 = 1/13.

practice.question: The probability that it will rain tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability that it will not rain tomorrow?
practice.explanation: Not raining is the complement of raining. P(not rain) = 1 - P(rain) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7.

practice.question: Two fair coins are tossed together. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
practice.explanation: Sample space = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, 4 equally likely outcomes. Exactly one head occurs in {HT, TH} = 2 outcomes. Probability = 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.explanation: Total outcomes = 6 x 6 = 36. Favorable pairs with sum 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) = 6 outcomes. Probability = 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.question: A box contains 3 defective and 7 non-defective bulbs. Two bulbs are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are non-defective?
questions.explanation: Total bulbs = 10. P(first non-defective)=7/10. Without replacement, remaining non-defective=6 out of 9. P(second non-defective | first non-defective)=6/9. So probability = (7/10)*(6/9)=42/90=7/15.
questions.provenance: Authored original question; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: From 1 to 30, a number is selected at random. What is the probability that it is divisible by 3 or 5?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 3 in 1-30: 10 numbers. Multiples of 5: 6 numbers. Multiples of both (15): 2 numbers {15,30}. Using union: (10 + 6 - 2)/30 = 14/30 = 7/15.
questions.provenance: Authored original question; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.
